---
title: "Jev vs ML: When Routing Rules Change"
date: 2026-10-01
categories: [AI, Machine Learning, Enterprise AI, Software Engineering]
---

Recently, I came across [Jev](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction), TypeSafe’s model for making structured decisions. My first reaction was: **do we really need another classifier?** A classifier assigns an input, such as a customer request, to a category.

For “I don’t recognise this ATM withdrawal”, a chatbot might draft a reply. A routing system needs a destination. Jev selects from predefined choices and reports how certain it is.

Traditional machine learning (ML) already handles classification well. Where would Jev help?

The interesting part turned out to be what happens **when the business changes the rules**.

## Same message, different destination

Imagine a bank routing requests into seven **business queues**: destinations for responsible teams or workflows. I called this initial set **V1**.

| V1 queue | What it handles |
|---|---|
| `CARD_SERVICES` | Card delivery, activation, PINs and administration |
| `CARD_PAYMENTS` | Card purchases and payment problems |
| `CASH_WITHDRAWAL` | ATM and withdrawal problems |
| `TRANSFERS` | Sending and receiving transfers |
| `TOP_UPS` | Adding money to an account |
| `ACCOUNT_ACCESS` | Account access and administration |
| `CURRENCY` | Currency support and exchange |

The bank then separates everyday service, security incidents and identity checks, and groups digital-payment problems together. The revised set, **V2**, has nine queues:

| V2 queue | What it handles |
|---|---|
| `CARD_MANAGEMENT` | Card issuance, activation, PINs and operation |
| `DIGITAL_PAYMENTS` | Card, contactless and mobile payments; refunds and charges |
| `CASH_WITHDRAWAL` | Ordinary ATM and withdrawal problems |
| `TRANSFERS` | Sending and receiving transfers |
| `TOP_UPS` | Adding money and related problems |
| `ACCOUNT_SERVICES` | Account access, personal details and administration |
| `IDENTITY_COMPLIANCE` | Verifying identity and where funds come from |
| `SECURITY_DISPUTES` | Unrecognised transactions, suspected compromise and lost or stolen cards or phones |
| `CURRENCY` | Currency support and exchange |

An ATM failing to dispense cash still goes to `CASH_WITHDRAWAL`. But our unrecognised withdrawal now goes to `SECURITY_DISPUTES`, because it needs a security investigation. The message hasn’t changed. **The correct destination has.**

## How I tested it

I used [PolyAI’s BANKING77 dataset from Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/PolyAI/banking77): 13,083 queries with 77 categories, split into 10,003 training and 3,080 test examples. I mapped them into V1/V2 queues and fixed a 600-request evaluation set.

Models received customer text, never the original intent or evaluation labels. Those stayed with the evaluator.

The key difference was **learning from examples versus selecting from descriptions**. A labelled example is a request with its correct queue recorded.

- **TF-IDF + Logistic Regression:** learns word patterns from labelled requests—“ATM” and “withdrawal”, for example. Despite its name, Logistic Regression assigns categories here; the tables shorten it to **LR**.
- **MiniLM embeddings + LR:** first represents meaning as numbers, called *embeddings*. This helps connect “my transfer hasn’t arrived” with “the recipient hasn’t received the money”. It then learns queues from labelled requests.
- **Qwen3-4B:** a small language model—a compact model trained on language—asked to choose a queue using its description.
- **Jev:** a model designed to choose between defined options, given the same queue descriptions.

**Accuracy** is the proportion correct. **Macro-F1** gives every queue equal weight and penalises both wrongly routed requests and missed cases; 1.0 is perfect. **p50 latency** is the median response time: half the decisions finish sooner, half later.

## Test 1: ordinary ML was already strong

The two classifiers that learn from labelled examples used all 10,003 V1 training requests.

| Model | Macro-F1 | Accuracy | p50 latency |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| TF-IDF + LR | **0.9588** | **0.9600** | **0.370 ms** |
| MiniLM + LR | 0.9508 | 0.9567 | 13.338 ms |

TF-IDF was slightly more accurate and about **36 times faster**. Distinctive banking words likely helped it.

It was a useful reminder for me: a newer model needs to earn its place.

## Test 2: change the queues

I reused historical training data for **transfers, top-ups and currency**, whose old queues still identified one clear destination. Where an old queue split across several new ones, I excluded those ambiguous labels.

For six affected V2 queues, I supplied **20 or 100 newly labelled requests per queue**: 120 or 600 total. I repeated each training condition with five different random samples. Qwen and Jev received the same V2 descriptions and **zero examples of correct V2 routing**, called “zero-shot”. Neither was retrained.

| Method | New V2 labels | Macro-F1 | Range across five runs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen3-4B | 0 | 0.7749 | — |
| **Jev** | **0** | **0.8954** | — |
| TF-IDF + LR | 120 | 0.6810 | 0.6549–0.7114 |
| MiniLM + LR | 120 | 0.8460 | 0.8261–0.8633 |
| TF-IDF + LR | 600 | 0.8864 | 0.8795–0.9003 |
| MiniLM + LR | 600 | **0.9065** | 0.8958–0.9172 |

![V2 Macro-F1 against the number of newly labelled examples. Jev scores 0.8954 with zero new labels; MiniLM plus Logistic Regression scores 0.9065 with 600. Vertical bars show supervised minimum-to-maximum ranges across five draws.](v2-label-efficiency.png)

With 120 labels, MiniLM beat TF-IDF by **16.5 Macro-F1 points**; at 600, the gap narrowed to two. Its existing knowledge of language appears useful when examples are scarce. The trained-classifier scores are five-run averages.

Jev surprised me: **0.8954 without new labels**, just 1.1 points below MiniLM with 600. A small gap doesn’t establish equivalent performance, but it makes Jev worth investigating.

Of requests Qwen sent to security, only **43.00%** belonged there, versus **95.24%** for Jev.

## Fast decisions, or fast adaptation?

| Method | Test | Observed p50 latency |
|---|---|---:|
| TF-IDF + LR | V1 | **0.370 ms** |
| MiniLM + LR | V1 | 13.338 ms |
| Jev API | V2 | 684.89 ms |
| Qwen3-4B local | V2 | 1,214.45 ms |

Jev’s 600 requests cost **$0.013691**, about **$0.0228 per 1,000 decisions**, excluding other operating costs. Qwen ran on my laptop; Jev used an online service, so timings reflect those deployments.

Traditional ML was much faster per request. Jev let me test changed rules without collecting new labels first. **I didn’t measure total adaptation time**; new descriptions still need testing before deployment.

## Confidence needs checking too

Jev gave its chosen queue an average probability of **94.43%**, but chose correctly **89.00%** of the time. It was somewhat overconfident.

But ranking requests by its confidence score revealed a useful review strategy:

| Lowest-confidence requests reviewed | Requests | Share of errors surfaced |
|---|---:|---:|
| 10% | 60 | 36.4% |
| **20%** | **120** | **59.1%** |
| 30% | 180 | 72.7% |

Reviewing one-fifth of requests would have surfaced nearly three-fifths of errors. I calculated this afterwards; I didn’t test whether reviewers would correct them.

**The model proposes a decision. Software decides what happens next.**

## What I would take into a real project

The results suggest four practical choices:

- **If the kinds of requests and the teams handling them rarely change, and you have many examples showing which team should handle each request:** start with TF-IDF + LR. It worked well here and responded quickly.
- **If responsibilities have changed and you can identify the right team for a small number of requests:** try MiniLM + LR. In this test, it learned which team should handle each request from fewer examples than TF-IDF + LR.
- **If you need to try a new set of teams before you have examples:** try Jev by describing what each team handles. Then compare its suggestions with choices made by people reviewing the requests.
- **If requests cannot be sent outside your organisation:** choose a model that runs on your own systems. Test how accurately and quickly it works with your requests.

I would also separate **what the customer needs** from **who handles it**. Store “unrecognised withdrawal”, rather than only “ATM team”. If that team changes, updating a routing table may be enough. My experiment assumed only the old queue labels were available for training.

These findings come from one simulated reorganisation, 600 test requests and one small language model configuration. Real tickets can be messier; models may also have encountered this public dataset before.

I started by asking whether we needed another classifier. I finished asking: **how often do our routing rules change—and how will we catch wrong decisions?**

<details>
<summary>Additional experiment details</summary>

MiniLM used `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (384-dimensional embeddings). Qwen used `Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507`, Q4_K_M quantisation through Ollama. Jev was requested as `jev-latest`; the API reported the serving model as `jev-1.13.0`. For V2, Logistic Regression used balanced class weights to account for unequal amounts of reusable historical data and newly labelled data. Zero-shot means no task examples were supplied for V2; both models still used pretrained knowledge and the class definitions.

Zero-shot V2 accuracy was 0.7767 for Qwen and 0.8900 for Jev. Their security-class results were:

| Model | Precision | Recall | F1 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen3-4B | 0.4300 | 0.9149 | 0.5850 |
| Jev | 0.9524 | 0.8511 | 0.8989 |

Jev consumed 325,972 input tokens. Its Expected Calibration Error was 5.85%: this summarises gaps between reported probability and observed correctness across probability bins. Among 499 predictions with probability between 0.9 and 1.0, mean probability was 98.87% and accuracy was 93.99%. Its [confidence score is derived from the probability distribution](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence), so it is not independent evidence of correctness. Review thresholds need fresh validation on the intended workload.

</details>

You can find my experiment source code on [GitHub](https://github.com/pengbin2015/jev-experiment/tree/main).
